periods.activity_title: What Does Your Number Say About Your Neighbours?

textbook_items_in_class.description: List five different situations in which numbers are used. Share and discuss with classmates.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: There are 5 children all of different heights. Can they stand such that four say '1' and the last says '0'? Why or why not?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: For a group of 5 children, is the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 possible?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.1 p.56
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 possible? Why or why not?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.1 p.56
homework.description: How would you rearrange the five children so that the maximum number of children say '2'?

time_bands.activity: Math Talk, section 3.1 p.55 ("List five different situations in which numbers are used...."). Students share orally; draw out examples where a number encodes a relationship rather than a count, establishing the idea that numbers can represent comparisons.

Introduce the height-neighbour scenario from section 3.1: each child in a line announces how many immediate neighbours are taller. Work through Figure it Out Q4, section 3.1 p.56 ("There are 5 children all of different heights....") and Figure it Out Q5, section 3.1 p.56 ("For a group of 5 children, is the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 possible?") as shared reasoning tasks, asking students to explain the structural constraints imposed by position and relative height.

Students work in pairs on Figure it Out Q6, section 3.1 p.56 ("Is the sequence 0, 1, 2, 1, 0 possible? Why or why not?"). Pairs draft a written justification using height-ordering logic; select two pairs to share contrasting arguments.

Whole-class consolidation: teacher asks students to state the rules that make certain sequences impossible — end-position constraint, neighbour-uniqueness, parity of 2-counts. Students record the generalised constraints in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is for students to treat the numbers as arbitrary labels rather than counts of taller neighbours — watch for justifications that do not invoke relative height at all. Building the constraint argument from the end-position rule (an end child has only one neighbour, so cannot say '2') is a productive anchor for the whole discussion. Figure it Out Q7, section 3.1 p.56 is set as reinforcement for students to attempt independently.

periods.activity_title: Discovering Why the Largest Must Always Win

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Colour or mark the supercells in the given table: 6828, 670, 9435, 3780, 3708, 7308, 8000, 5583, 52.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell? Can the cell with the smallest number be a supercell? Why or why not?
Can you fill a supercell table without repeating numbers such that there are no supercells? Why or why not?

time_bands.activity: Introduce the supercell definition from section 3.2: a cell whose number is strictly greater than all its adjacent cells. Use Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.57 ("Colour or mark the supercells in the given table: 6828, 670, 9435....") — students identify which cells qualify and explain adjacency in a row.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58 ("Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell?...") in pairs, constructing a written argument. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'What happens if the largest number sits between two neighbours — can either neighbour be larger than it?'

Class investigates Try This Q6, section 3.2 p.58 ("Can you fill a supercell table without repeating numbers such that there are no supercells?..."). Groups attempt to construct a counter-example; whole class discusses why the attempt always fails — the largest number in any arrangement must beat all its neighbours.

Students articulate in one sentence: why the largest number is always a supercell and why the smallest never can be. Teacher records the class-constructed reasoning on the board as a shared proof statement.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 'adjacent' with 'in the same row'; extend the conversation to clarify that in a 2-D grid adjacency includes cells above and below, not just left and right. The crucial reasoning move — if a cell has the maximum value, no neighbour can exceed it — is worth dwelling on until every student can articulate it. Try This Q6 is an excellent vehicle for this: the impossibility of a no-supercell table follows directly from the maximum-value argument.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells (given seed values 5346, 1258, 9635).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 3.2 p.57
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill the table to get as many supercells as possible using numbers between 100 and 1000 without repetitions.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.2 p.58
textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill a table such that the cell having the second largest number is not a supercell.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 3.2 p.58
homework.description: Fill a table such that the second largest number is not a supercell but the second smallest number is a supercell. Is it possible?

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57 ("Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells...."). The task demands deliberate placement: coloured cells must exceed their neighbours, uncoloured cells must not.

Groups of three tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 3.2 p.57 ("Fill the table to get as many supercells as possible using numbers between 100 and 1000 without repetitions."). Groups record their maximum count and the arrangement used, then compare with another group to see whether a higher count is achievable.

Pairs attempt Figure it Out Q8, section 3.2 p.58 ("Fill a table such that the cell having the second largest number is not a supercell."). Students explain the arrangement they used and why placing the second-largest adjacent to the largest blocks its supercell status.

Quick share: each group states one insight about how placement — not just magnitude — determines supercell status. Teacher names Figure it Out Q9, section 3.2 p.58 as an extended challenge to explore independently.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that the largest number is always a supercell and the smallest never is, students now discover that intermediate numbers can be strategically placed to be supercells or not. The key error to watch for is students who fill a table randomly and then retrospectively check — encourage planning from the target supercell positions outward. Figure it Out Q9, section 3.2 p.58 is assigned as homework for students ready to push further.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line

periods.activity_title: Landing Large Numbers at the Right Spot

textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales and label the remaining positions. Sub-parts: (a) scale of 5, around 2010–2020; (b) scale of 1, around 9996–9997; (c) scale of 1, around 15077–15083; (d) scale of 1000, around 86705–87705. Circle smallest and box largest in each.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws a number line on the board spanning 1000 to 10,000 and invites students to estimate where 2180, 5030, and 9590 (from the section 3.3 opening set) would land. Discuss how the scale interval determines precision of placement.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.59 ("Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales....") sub-parts (a)–(d). For each sub-part they identify the scale, read the given tick labels, interpolate or extrapolate to name the marked positions, and label the remaining ones. They then circle the smallest and box the largest in each.

Pairs compare answers for sub-part (d) (scale of 1000): a scale-of-1000 number line requires reasoning about which thousand-interval a number falls in. Students justify their placements to each other by naming the bounding tick values.
Class review: teacher highlights the sub-part where most disagreement arose. Students state aloud the rule for reading an intermediate tick when the scale is not 1.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is reading a number line as if all scales are 1; students who mis-identify the interval between ticks will misplace every number on that sub-part. Emphasise computing the gap from two known tick labels before placing anything. The supercell logic from section 3.2 reappears quietly in the 5-digit completion table described in the section — connecting that visual to the supercell definition helps students who found the grid work compelling.
materials: Ruler (optional, for drawing neat number lines)

periods.activity_title: Digit Sums, Patterns, and the Detective's Notebook

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find out how many numbers have two digits, three digits, four digits, and five digits. Complete the table.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60
textbook_items_in_class.description: Digit sum 14: (a) write other numbers whose digits add up to 14; (b) what is the smallest number with digit sum 14? (c) what is the largest 5-digit number with digit sum 14? (d) how big a number can you form with digit sum 14?
Digit Detectives: among numbers 1–100, how many times does the digit '7' occur? Among 1–1000?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.4 p.60
homework.description: Find out the digit sums of all numbers from 40 to 70 and share observations.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.60 ("Find out how many numbers have two digits, three digits, four digits, and five digits...."). Establish the pattern 9, 90, 900, 9000, 90000 through the table before proceeding.

Introduce Komal's observation from section 3.4 that different numbers can share digit sum 14 (68, 176, 545). Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 3.4 p.60 ("Digit sum 14: write other numbers, find smallest and largest....") parts (a)–(d). The reasoning task — why the largest number with digit sum 14 can be made arbitrarily long by inserting 0s — is highlighted in discussion.

Digit Detectives task: Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.61 ("Among numbers 1–100, how many times does the digit '7' occur? Among 1–1000?"). Students work in pairs, organising a systematic count by units-place and tens-place separately, then extend the argument to 1–1000 by reasoning about hundreds-place occurrences.
Each pair shares their count and strategy. Teacher distinguishes two common approaches — exhaustive listing vs. structured counting — and discusses which scales to each range.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently undercount digit occurrences because they scan numbers visually rather than by place. The tens-place argument for 70–79 (ten 7s) and units-place argument for 7, 17, 27, …, 97 (ten 7s) must be separated clearly. Figure it Out Q2, section 3.4 p.60 is assigned as homework to build fluency with digit-sum patterns across a consecutive range.

periods.activity_title: Reversing, Adding, and Reasoning About Palindromes

textbook_items_in_class.description: Write all possible 3-digit palindromes using the digits 1, 2, and 3.
Will reversing and adding numbers repeatedly, starting with a 2-digit number, always give a palindrome? Explore and find out.
Puzzle time: I am a 5-digit palindrome, odd, with 't' digit double 'u' digit and 'h' digit double 't' digit. Who am I?

time_bands.activity: Students examine the palindrome examples from section 3.5 (66, 848, 575, 797, 1111) and articulate the defining property. They complete Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.61 ("Write all possible 3-digit palindromes using the digits 1, 2, and 3.") — working systematically through first-digit choices to ensure no case is missed.

Introduce the reverse-and-add procedure through the section's three worked examples. Students then explore Math Talk, section 3.5 p.62 ("Will reversing and adding numbers repeatedly, starting with a 2-digit number, always give a palindrome?...") by testing at least four 2-digit starting numbers and recording the number of steps to a palindrome.

Pairs tackle Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.62 ("Puzzle time: I am a 5-digit palindrome, odd, with 't' digit double 'u' digit and 'h' digit double 't' digit...."). Students reason from the constraint chain: if u = d, t = 2d, h = 4d, and the number is a palindrome (h t u t h form), what digit values keep each place a single digit?

Class share: students state what palindrome symmetry means for the digit constraints in the puzzle and confirm whether any solution they found is odd. Teacher notes the connection between palindrome structure and the constraint that h = first digit = last digit.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly miss palindromes in the 3-digit listing task by not working systematically — a first-digit then middle-digit approach prevents omissions. For the reverse-and-add exploration, watch for students who stop after one addition and do not repeat the process when the result is not yet a palindrome. The puzzle requires simultaneous reasoning about place-value notation and palindrome symmetry; prompting students to write the palindrome as 'h t u t h' before substituting the ratio constraints usually unlocks the path.

textbook_items_in_class.description: Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps (form largest A and smallest B from digits, compute C = A − B, repeat). Find out what always happens.
Carry out the same Kaprekar steps with a few 3-digit numbers. What number starts repeating?
Find all possible times on a 12-hour clock of the type 4:44 (repeated digit), 10:10 (two pairs), and 12:21 (palindrome time).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65
homework.description: How many rounds does the number 5683 take to reach the Kaprekar constant (6174)?

time_bands.activity: Walk through the two complete Kaprekar iterations from section 3.6 starting from 6382. Students then each choose a different 4-digit number and apply the process — Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.63 ("Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps....") — recording each iteration until a repeat is reached.

Students apply the same procedure to a 3-digit number of their choice — Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.63 ("Carry out the same Kaprekar steps with a few 3-digit numbers. What number starts repeating?"). Class pools results to identify 495 as the 3-digit analogue of 6174.

Transition to section 3.7. Students work on Figure it Out, section 3.7 p.64 ("Find all possible times on a 12-hour clock of the type 4:44, 10:10, and 12:21...."). They list candidates systematically by first fixing the hour and then checking valid minute values for each palindrome type.

Pairs compare their palindromic time lists, resolve any disagreements, and note which hour yields the most palindromic readings. Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65 is set as homework — students will count Kaprekar rounds for 5683 independently.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error in the Kaprekar procedure is forgetting to pad the result with a leading zero when C has fewer than four digits — for example, 0999 must be treated as a 4-digit number so the next iteration's rearrangements are correct. In the clock task, students sometimes overlook times like 1:11 or 2:22 because they focus only on palindrome structure and miss the repeated-digit type; encouraging a systematic list by type prevents this. Figure it Out Q4, section 3.7 p.65 is a natural homework extension for students who finished the Kaprekar work quickly.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Using four chosen digits, make the smallest and largest 4-digit numbers: (a) make the difference greater than 5085; (b) make the difference less than 5085; (c) make the sum greater than 9779; (d) make the sum less than 9779.

Spider-web mental math: the numbers in the middle column (400, 1500, 13000, 25000, 28000, 61600) can be added (each used as many times as needed) to reach target sums on the sides. Draw arrows to show which central numbers combine to make each target.
Adding and subtracting with the boxes (40000, 300, 7000, 1500, 12000, 800): use addition and subtraction to reach 45000, 5900, 17500, and 21400.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.64 ("Using four chosen digits, make the smallest and largest 4-digit numbers....") parts (a)–(d). The task uses the digit-rearrangement idea from the Kaprekar section in a new context — maximising or minimising differences and sums by choice of digit set.

Introduce the spider-web figure from section 3.8. Students attempt Figure it Out, section 3.8 p.65 ("Spider-web mental math: numbers in the middle column can be added to reach target sums on the sides....") by reasoning about which multiples or combinations of the central values reach each target without a column algorithm.

Students extend to Figure it Out, section 3.8 p.66 ("Adding and subtracting with the boxes: use addition and subtraction to reach 45000, 5900, 17500, and 21400."). Pairs share their combinations, noting where a subtraction shortcut simplifies what would otherwise be a long addition chain.

Quick oral round: teacher names a target, students call out a combination strategy. Emphasise that mental arithmetic uses number sense — choosing the closest large value first then adjusting — rather than left-to-right computation.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with digit rearrangements in the Kaprekar context, students now apply the same thinking to choosing a digit set that maximises or minimises an arithmetic outcome — the link between the two ideas is worth naming. In the spider-web task, a frequent error is trying only one central number at a time; prompt students to consider pairs and triples of values from the outset. Math Talk, section 3.8 p.66 (which numbers cannot be reached as thousands) is a natural extension if time permits.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Digit-Count Outcomes and Counting Arrays Cleverly

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67
textbook_items_in_class.description: Always, Sometimes, Never? (a) 5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (b) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 4-digit number; (c) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 6-digit number; (d) 5-digit − 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (e) 5-digit − 2-digit gives a 3-digit number.

Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond arrangement of 15s, 25s, and 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2 (125, 250, 500, 1000). Sub-parts (a)–(f).

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67 ("Always, Sometimes, Never?..."). For each statement they construct an example confirming the labelled case and, where the answer is 'sometimes', a counter-example for the other case — turning a classification task into a reasoning exercise.

Introduce section 3.9's key question: is one-by-one addition always necessary? Students work through Figure it Out, section 3.9 p.67 ("Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays....") sub-parts (a)–(f). For each array they first identify how many of each value appear, multiply, then add the products — comparing this with the one-by-one sum to verify.

Pairs share contrasting strategies for sub-part (f) (powers of 2 diamond). Class discusses why counting-and-multiplying is more efficient than sequential addition, and what property of the array makes the shortcut work — the array is a repeated pattern, not an arbitrary collection.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes answer 'never' to the statement '5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit number' without verifying — 99999 + 00001 = 100000 shows a carry, but 10000 + 10000 = 20000 shows no carry, making the answer 'sometimes'; prompt them to test boundary cases. In the array task, the efficiency of counting-then-multiplying is the section's key insight — ensure students articulate why it works (each occurrence contributes its own value) rather than accepting it as a trick.

textbook_segments.title: An Unsolved Mystery — the Collatz Conjecture!

periods.activity_title: Why Shortcuts Work, and a Conjecture No One Has Proved

textbook_items_in_class.description: Make Collatz sequences starting from your favourite whole numbers. Do you always reach 1? Do you believe Collatz's conjecture? Why or why not?

time_bands.activity: Brief whole-class discussion: from the array-counting work in section 3.9, students articulate in their own words why multiplying count × value gives the correct array sum. Teacher connects this reasoning to the Math Talk prompt from section 3.9 — sharing different strategies.

Introduce the Collatz rule from section 3.10: halve if even; multiply by 3 and add 1 if odd; repeat. Walk through one of the four illustrative sequences from the section. Students independently generate Collatz sequences for at least three self-chosen whole numbers — Figure it Out, section 3.10 p.69 ("Make Collatz sequences starting from your favourite whole numbers....") — and record the length of each sequence to 1.

Students compare sequence lengths and discuss: does every sequence seem to reach 1? Can anyone find a counter-example? Class considers what 'proof' would mean here — why testing many cases is not the same as proving all cases — using the section's framing that the conjecture has been open since 1937.

Students write one sentence each: 'I believe / do not believe the Collatz conjecture because…', mirroring the Figure it Out prompt. Two or three share; teacher notes that mathematicians worldwide share this uncertainty.

periods.teacher_notes: The Collatz section's pedagogical purpose is explicitly one of mathematical reasoning about conjecture — not algorithm execution — so ensure the discussion does not collapse into 'let's compute more examples' without the accompanying reflection on what certainty in mathematics requires. A common confusion is applying the odd rule to even numbers or vice versa; a quick check of the rule before students begin their own sequences prevents cascading errors. The reasoning about why counting-times-value works for arrays (from section 3.9) is a useful warmup because it models exactly the move — from observed pattern to stated justification — that the Collatz discussion then asks for at a harder level.

periods.activity_title: How Many Steps, Blinks, and Breaths? Estimating Real Magnitudes

textbook_items_in_class.description: Estimate the number of steps to walk: (a) to the classroom door; (b) across the school ground; (c) from classroom to school gate; (d) from school to home.
Estimate the number of times you blink or the number of breaths you take: (a) in a minute; (b) in an hour; (c) in a day.

Quick 30-second estimate questions: (1) number of words in the maths textbook — more or less than 5000? (2) school students travelling by bus — more or less than 200? (3) Does Roshan's ₹100 estimate for fruit custard for 5 people seem right? (4) Estimate the Gandhinagar–Kohima distance. (5) Has Sheetal spent around 13,000 hours in school? (6) Estimate walking time to a favourite place, a neighbouring state capital, and tip-to-tip India. (7) Make your own estimation questions.

time_bands.activity: Present Paromita's estimate from section 3.11 (32+29+35 ≈ 100 per class × 5 classes ≈ 500). Students discuss the method: round each quantity to a convenient value, multiply by a count, state the estimate with a justification. Establish that a good estimate names its assumptions.

Students work on Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.69 ("Estimate the number of steps to walk....") and Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.70 ("Estimate the number of times you blink or breaths you take...."). For each, they state the unit rate (steps per metre, blinks per minute) they assumed and then scale it.

Rapid-fire round using Figure it Out, section 3.11 p.70 ("Quick 30-second estimate questions...."). Students work in pairs on questions 1–5, each pair committing to a 'more' or 'less' answer with a one-line justification. Pairs then design one original estimation question (question 7) and challenge another pair.

Gallery of original estimation questions: three or four pairs share theirs. Class rapidly votes on whether each is more or less than a proposed benchmark, and the proposing pair reveals their own estimate and reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: Students tend to either over-precision (computing exact values) or under-justification (guessing without a stated rate). The core skill is naming a plausible unit rate and scaling it — watch for estimates with no stated assumption, and ask 'what did you assume about one minute of blinking?' to draw out the reasoning. Section 3.11 is also a good place to connect to the digit-count work from section 3.4: estimating the number of words in a textbook uses the same 'count a unit, multiply by the number of units' logic that underpinned the array sums in section 3.9.

periods.activity_title: Winning Strategies: A Chapter Synthesis Through Number Games

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.12 p.72
textbook_items_in_class.description: Try This: there is only one supercell in the given 3×3 grid (16200, 39344, 29765 / 23609, 62871, 45306 / 19381, 50319, 38408). Exchange two digits of one number to create exactly 4 supercells. Figure out which digits to swap.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73
textbook_items_in_class.description: Starting with 0, players alternate adding numbers between 1 and 3. The first person to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy now?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 3.12 p.72
textbook_items_in_class.description: Recall the powers of 2 from Chapter 1. Why is the Collatz conjecture correct for all starting numbers in this sequence?

time_bands.activity: Pairs play the section 3.12 Game #1 (alternately add 1–3 to a running total; reach 21 to win) three times, swapping who goes first. After play, students identify which totals are 'safe positions' — totals from which the player who just reached them can guarantee a win regardless of the opponent's move.

Whole-class derive the winning strategy for Game #1. Then students attempt Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73 ("Starting with 0, players alternate adding numbers between 1 and 3. The first person to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy now?") — the target changes from 21 to 22, requiring them to re-derive the safe positions and determine which player wins with perfect play.

Synthesis connections: students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 3.12 p.72 ("Exchange two digits of one number to create exactly 4 supercells....") drawing on the supercell reasoning established in section 3.2, and Figure it Out Q8, section 3.12 p.72 ("Why is the Collatz conjecture correct for all starting numbers that are powers of 2?") drawing on the Collatz reasoning from section 3.10. Each question reconnects a concept from earlier in the chapter.

Students write a two-sentence 'chapter insight': one thing they now know how to reason about that they did not at the start, naming the concept (digit sums, palindromes, Kaprekar constant, Collatz, estimation, supercells, or game strategy). Two or three share aloud. Teacher draws the thread: all of these activities used the same move — finding and naming the pattern that makes a result inevitable.

periods.teacher_notes: The game strategy task is the chapter's clearest instance of formal reasoning: students must identify invariant safe positions rather than playing by feel. A common error is concluding that 'first player always wins' or 'second player always wins' without specifying the target — when the target changes from 21 to 22, the winning player flips; watch for students who carry over the Game #1 answer without re-deriving. The supercell digit-swap in Figure it Out Q1 and the Collatz powers-of-2 explanation in Figure it Out Q8 draw together reasoning threads from across the chapter, making this a genuine synthesis rather than new content.

Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond arrangement of 15s, 25s, and 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2 (125, 250, 500, 1000). Sub-parts (a)–(f).

Quick 30-second estimate questions: (1) number of words in the maths textbook — more or less than 5000? (2) school students travelling by bus — more or less than 200? (3) Does Roshan's ₹100 estimate for fruit custard for 5 people seem right? (4) Estimate the Gandhinagar–Kohima distance. (5) Has Sheetal spent around 13,000 hours in school? items.prompt: Six children of different heights stand in a row. The child at the left end says '1'. Explain why a child standing at either end of the row can never say '2', no matter how the children are arranged.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A child at either end of the row has exactly one immediate neighbour, so at most one neighbour can be taller than them. The number a child says counts only immediate neighbours who are taller, so the maximum value an end child can announce is 1, never 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the position constraint: end children have only one neighbour, capping their count of taller neighbours at 1.

inclusivity.support: Re-read the height-neighbour rule and count the neighbours of the first child in a row of three.
inclusivity.challenge: Describe what sequences of numbers are possible for a row of exactly four children of different heights, and justify each case.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 3.1 p.56
exercise.description: For a group of 5 children, is the sequence 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 possible?

items.prompt: A row contains seven different numbers. Explain why the cell holding the largest number in the row must always be a supercell, and why the cell holding the smallest number can never be a supercell.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The largest number exceeds every other number in the row, so it is greater than both its adjacent neighbours — making it a supercell by definition. The smallest number is less than every other number, so at least one of its neighbours is larger than it — which means it fails the supercell condition.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the supercell definition: a cell must exceed all adjacent cells; the maximum always does, the minimum never does.

inclusivity.support: Write out the supercell definition and check it for the largest and smallest cells in a row of five numbers you choose.
inclusivity.challenge: Construct a row of six numbers where exactly three cells are supercells, and explain the placement rule you used.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.2 p.58
exercise.description: Will the cell with the largest number always be a supercell? Can the cell with the smallest number be a supercell? Why or why not?

items.prompt: Among the whole numbers from 1 to 100, how many times does the digit 7 appear in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20. The digit 7 appears in the units place in 7, 17, 27, 37, 47, 57, 67, 77, 87, 97 — ten times. It appears in the tens place in 70, 71, 72, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79 — ten times. The number 77 contributes once to each group. Total = 10 + 10 = 20.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count units-place 7s (ten occurrences: 7, 17, …, 97) and tens-place 7s (ten occurrences: 70–79) separately, then add.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted only units-place occurrences (7, 17, 27, …, 97) and missed the tens-place group entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student counted one group of ten correctly but subtracted 77 once, mistakenly treating the double-7 as a duplication rather than two separate digit occurrences.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student counted 19 by adding the two groups but subtracting 77 once, not realising 77 contributes two 7-digits, not one extra.

inclusivity.support: List all numbers from 1 to 30 that contain the digit 3, and count each occurrence separately.
inclusivity.challenge: Extend the argument: how many times does the digit 7 appear among the numbers from 1 to 1000? Justify by place.

exercise.description: Digit Detectives: among numbers 1–100, how many times does the digit '7' occur? Among 1–1000?

items.prompt: A 5-digit palindrome has the property that its hundreds digit is double its units digit, and its thousands digit is double its hundreds digit. The number is odd. Identify the number and explain how the palindrome structure constrains which digit values are possible.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A 5-digit palindrome has the form h t u t h (first = last, second = fourth). So the digits are h, t, u, t, h. Given h = 2t and t = 2u, we have h = 4u. For each digit to be a single digit (0–9): if u = 1, t = 2, h = 4, giving the palindrome 42124 — but this is even. If u = 1, t = 2, h = 4 and the number is 42124, the units digit is 4 (even). For the number to be odd, its units (last) digit must be odd. The last digit equals h = 4u, so 4u must be odd — impossible since 4u is always even. However, re-reading: the palindrome is h t u t h, so the units (last) digit is h. For h to be odd, 4u must be odd, which is impossible for integer u. Re-checking: the puzzle states 'h digit = double t digit; t digit = double u digit' meaning h = 2t and t = 2u, with the palindrome written as h-t-u-t-h. The only single-digit solution is u=1, t=2, h=4 giving 42124, which is even. The alternative reading (u digit = 2 × t digit, t digit = 2 × h digit) gives h=1, t=2, u=4, palindrome 12421, units digit 1 — odd. So the answer is 12421.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the 5-digit palindrome as h-t-u-t-h, apply the ratio constraints to find h=1, t=2, u=4, and verify 12421 is odd.

inclusivity.support: Write a 5-digit palindrome as _ _ _ _ _ and mark which positions must match; then substitute small values for the middle digit.
inclusivity.challenge: Are there other 5-digit palindromes where adjacent digits are in a 1:2 ratio? Describe all possibilities systematically.

exercise.description: Puzzle time: I am a 5-digit palindrome, odd, with 't' digit double 'u' digit and 'h' digit double 't' digit. Who am I?

items.prompt: A rectangular array contains 4 rows and 5 columns. Every cell in the first two rows holds the number 30, and every cell in the last two rows holds the number 60. A student says: 'I can find the total without adding all twenty numbers one by one.' Explain the student's reasoning and give the total.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There are 4 × 5 = 20 cells. The first two rows contain 2 × 5 = 10 cells each holding 30, contributing 10 × 30 = 300. The last two rows contain 2 × 5 = 10 cells each holding 60, contributing 10 × 60 = 600. Total = 300 + 600 = 900. The student's reasoning is to count how many of each repeated value appear and multiply, rather than adding individually.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count occurrences of each repeated value, multiply each count by its value, and sum the products.

inclusivity.support: Count how many 30s appear in just the first row, then use multiplication to extend to both rows.
inclusivity.challenge: Design a 3×6 array using three different repeated values whose total is exactly 504, and show your reasoning.

exercise.description: Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond arrangement of 15s, 25s, and 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2 (125, 250, 500, 1000). Sub-parts (a)–(f).

items.prompt: Two players take turns adding a whole number from 1 to 3 to a running total that starts at 0. The player who reaches exactly 22 wins. Which player has a winning strategy — the one who goes first or the one who goes second? Describe the strategy and explain why it guarantees a win.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first player has the winning strategy. The key is to identify 'safe positions' — totals from which the player who just moved can guarantee a win. Since each turn adds 1, 2, or 3, a sum of 4 added per two-player cycle is the invariant. Work backwards from 22: the second-to-last safe position is 22 − 4 = 18, then 14, 10, 6, 2. The first player should move to 2 on the first turn (adding 2). Thereafter, whatever the opponent adds (call it k, where k ∈ {1,2,3}), the first player adds (4 − k) to reach the next safe position: 6, 10, 14, 18, 22. Since 22 ÷ 4 = 5 remainder 2 and 2 is reachable on turn 1, the first player wins.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work backwards from 22 in steps of 4 to identify safe positions (2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22); the first player reaches 2 immediately and maintains the pattern by always adding the complement of the opponent's move to 4.

inclusivity.support: Play the game to 12 first (with 1–3 moves), try both players, and record which totals one player always tries to hit.
inclusivity.challenge: If the target changes to 25, which player wins and what are the new safe positions? Justify your answer.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 3.12 p.73
exercise.description: Starting with 0, players alternate adding numbers between 1 and 3. The first person to reach 22 wins. What is the winning strategy now?

items.prompt: Consider the following row of five numbers: 3140, 5820, 4700, 6310, 2980. How many supercells does this row contain? List each supercell and briefly explain why it qualifies.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Check each cell against its immediate neighbours. 3140: left end; only right neighbour is 5820. 3140 < 5820, so not a supercell. 5820: neighbours are 3140 and 4700. 5820 > 3140 and 5820 > 4700, so 5820 is a supercell. 4700: neighbours are 5820 and 6310. 4700 < 5820, so not a supercell. 6310: neighbours are 4700 and 2980. 6310 > 4700 and 6310 > 2980, so 6310 is a supercell. 2980: right end; only left neighbour is 6310. 2980 < 6310, so not a supercell. The row contains 2 supercells: 5820 and 6310.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each cell with all its immediate neighbours; mark it a supercell only if it strictly exceeds every neighbour.

inclusivity.support: For each number, write down only its immediate left and right neighbours, then check whether the number is bigger than both.
inclusivity.challenge: Rearrange these five numbers so that exactly three cells become supercells. State your arrangement and verify it.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.2 p.57
exercise.description: Fill the table with only 4-digit numbers such that the supercells are exactly the pre-coloured cells (given seed values 5346, 1258, 9635).

items.section_title: Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line
items.prompt: A number line has tick marks at regular intervals. The leftmost tick is labelled 4200 and the rightmost tick is labelled 4600. There are exactly four equal intervals between them (five tick marks in total). A point P is marked exactly at the third tick from the left. What number does P represent? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The total span is 4600 − 4200 = 400. With four equal intervals, each interval is 400 ÷ 4 = 100. The tick marks from left to right are 4200, 4300, 4400, 4500, 4600. The third tick from the left is 4400. P = 4400.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the interval size (total span ÷ number of intervals) and count up from the left endpoint.

inclusivity.support: First find the gap between the two labelled ends, then divide by the number of spaces between ticks.
inclusivity.challenge: If a new point Q is placed halfway between P and the rightmost tick, what number does Q represent? Justify your answer.

exercise.description: Identify the numbers marked on four number lines at different scales and label the remaining positions. Sub-parts: (a) scale of 5, around 2010–2020; (b) scale of 1, around 9996–9997; (c) scale of 1, around 15077–15083; (d) scale of 1000, around 86705–87705. Circle smallest and box largest in each.

items.prompt: Apply the Kaprekar process to the 4-digit number 3456. Show each step: form the largest and smallest rearrangements, subtract, and repeat until the result no longer changes. What is the final constant, and how many steps did it take?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step 1: Digits of 3456 are 3, 4, 5, 6. Largest = 6543, Smallest = 3456. C = 6543 − 3456 = 3087. Step 2: Digits of 3087 are 0, 3, 7, 8. Largest = 8730, Smallest = 0378 = 0378. C = 8730 − 0378 = 8352. Step 3: Digits of 8352 are 2, 3, 5, 8. Largest = 8532, Smallest = 2358. C = 8532 − 2358 = 6174. Step 4: Digits of 6174 are 1, 4, 6, 7. Largest = 7641, Smallest = 1467. C = 7641 − 1467 = 6174. The constant 6174 is reached at step 3 (since applying the process to 6174 returns 6174, confirming it is the fixed point). It took 3 steps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: At each step arrange the digits in descending and ascending order, subtract, and repeat; the process converges to 6174.

inclusivity.support: Write the digits of your number from largest to smallest to get A, then from smallest to largest to get B, and compute A − B.
inclusivity.challenge: Apply the same process starting from 8208 and count the steps to reach 6174; compare with the steps needed from 3456.

exercise.description: Take different 4-digit numbers and carry out the Kaprekar steps (form largest A and smallest B from digits, compute C = A − B, repeat). Find out what always happens.

items.prompt: Using the four digits 1, 3, 5, 7 (each used exactly once), form the smallest and largest possible 4-digit numbers. Then compute: (a) their difference, and (b) their sum. Is the difference greater than 5085? Is the sum greater than 9779?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Smallest 4-digit number from 1, 3, 5, 7: arrange in ascending order → 1357. Largest: arrange in descending order → 7531. (a) Difference: 7531 − 1357 = 6174. 6174 > 5085, so yes, the difference is greater than 5085. (b) Sum: 7531 + 1357 = 8888. 8888 < 9779, so no, the sum is not greater than 9779.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange digits in ascending order for the smallest and descending order for the largest, then subtract and add.

inclusivity.support: Write all four digits in a row from smallest to largest to get the smallest number, and from largest to smallest to get the largest.
inclusivity.challenge: Find a set of four different digits (none of them zero) whose largest-minus-smallest difference exceeds 7000. Justify your choice.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.64
exercise.description: Using four chosen digits, make the smallest and largest 4-digit numbers: (a) make the difference greater than 5085; (b) make the difference less than 5085; (c) make the sum greater than 9779; (d) make the sum less than 9779.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements about digit-count outcomes is ALWAYS true?

options.label: A
options.text: Adding a 5-digit number and a 5-digit number gives a 6-digit result.

options.label: B
options.text: Subtracting a 5-digit number from a different 5-digit number gives a 5-digit result.

options.label: C
options.text: Adding a 4-digit number and a 2-digit number gives a 4-digit or 5-digit result.

options.label: D
options.text: Subtracting a 2-digit number from a 5-digit number gives a 3-digit result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: C. A 4-digit number ranges from 1000 to 9999 and a 2-digit number from 10 to 99. Their sum ranges from 1010 to 10098. Sums up to 9999 are 4-digit; sums from 10000 onward are 5-digit. So the result is always either 4-digit or 5-digit — never 3-digit or 6-digit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the minimum and maximum possible sums (1000+10=1010 and 9999+99=10098) to confirm the result falls in the 4-digit or 5-digit range.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student assumes 5-digit + 5-digit always carries into a 6th digit, forgetting that 10000 + 10000 = 20000 (6-digit) but 10000 + 10001 = 20001 (5-digit) — wait, both are 5-digit; the error is overgeneralising from cases that do produce a carry.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student believes subtracting two 5-digit numbers always yields a 5-digit result, overlooking that 10001 − 10000 = 1, a 1-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student assumes a 5-digit minus 2-digit always gives a 3-digit result, ignoring that 99999 − 10 = 99989, which is still 5 digits.

inclusivity.support: Test each option with two specific examples — one that seems to confirm it and one that might break it.
inclusivity.challenge: For option A, find the exact conditions (boundary values) under which 5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit result versus a 6-digit result.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 3.8 p.67
exercise.description: Always, Sometimes, Never? (a) 5-digit + 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (b) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 4-digit number; (c) 4-digit + 2-digit gives a 6-digit number; (d) 5-digit − 5-digit gives a 5-digit number; (e) 5-digit − 2-digit gives a 3-digit number.

items.prompt: A diamond-shaped arrangement contains 1 copy of 100 at the centre, 4 copies of 50 around it, and 8 copies of 25 in the outer ring. Find the total sum of all numbers in the arrangement. Show your method.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count occurrences of each distinct value, multiply each count by its value, and add the three products.

inclusivity.support: Add up all the 25s first by counting them; then do the same for the 50s and the 100.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the outer ring to 8 copies of a new value so that the total of the whole arrangement becomes exactly 700. What is the new outer value?

exercise.description: Find the sum of numbers in six patterned arrays: (a) 3×4 grid of 40s and 50s; (b) 3×5 grid of 40s and 50s; (c) 4×4 grid of 32s; (d) 4×4 grid of 32s and 64s; (e) diamond arrangement of 15s, 25s, and 35s; (f) diamond of powers of 2 (125, 250, 500, 1000). Sub-parts (a)–(f).

items.prompt: A school library has 40 shelves. Each shelf holds approximately 30 books. Estimate the total number of books in the library. Then estimate how many of those books could be read in a year if a student reads about 2 books per month. Show your reasoning at each step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total books in library: 40 shelves × 30 books per shelf = 1200 books. Books readable in a year: 2 books per month × 12 months = 24 books per year. The estimates rest on the stated unit rates; any answer using reasonable rates with consistent multiplication is acceptable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: State a unit rate, multiply by the count of units, and carry the result forward as the input to the next estimation step.

inclusivity.support: First estimate books on one shelf, then think about how to use that to get the total for all shelves.
inclusivity.challenge: At the rate of 24 books per year, estimate how many years it would take one student to read every book in the library, and comment on whether that is a realistic goal.
